q: 1. The moment of inertia of a square of side (a) about an axis through its centre of gravity is
explain: Using the formula for a rectangle (bd³/12), where b=a and d=a, the MI of a square is (a * a³) / 12 = a^4 / 12.

q: 2. The C.G. of a solid right circular cone lies on the axis at a height
options: half of the total height above the base
one-third of the total height above the base
one-fourth of the total height above the base
explain: As established in Q6, the CG of a solid cone is located at h/4 from the base.

q: 3. The C.G. of a thin hollow hemisphere is at a distance of
explain: The CG of a hollow hemispherical shell lies exactly at the midpoint of the central radius, which is r/2 from the base.

q: 4. The C.G. of a solid cone lies on the central axis at a distance of
options: 1/3 of the total height above base
half the total height above base
1/4 of the total height above base
2/5 of the total height above base
explain: Repeated concept: Solid cone CG is at h/4 from the base.

q: 5. The C.G. of a hollow cylinder lies on the vertical axis above base at a distance of
explain: Due to symmetry, the CG of any cylinder (solid or hollow) lies at the geometric center, which is h/2 from the base.

q: 6. M.O.I. of a triangular section about an axis passing through its base is given by
explain: While the MI about the centroidal axis is bh³/36, using the parallel axis theorem, the MI about the base is bh³/12.

q: 7. M.O.I. of a solid cone about its vertical axis is
explain: The mass moment of inertia of a solid right circular cone about its longitudinal (vertical) axis is (3/10)Mr².

q: 8. M.O.I. of a solid circular cylinder about vertical axis is
explain: A cylinder viewed from the top is a circle; its mass moment of inertia about the central longitudinal axis is the same as a disk: (1/2)Mr².

q: 9. M.O.I. of elliptical section, of major axis = D and minor axis = B, is
explain: For an ellipse with axes B and D, the area MI about the major axis (D) is πBD³/64 (analogous to bd³/12).

q: 10. The moment of inertia of a triangle (having base = b and height = h) with respect to an axis through the apex and parallel to the base is
explain: Using Parallel Axis Theorem: I_apex = I_cg + A(d)². d = 2h/3. I_apex = bh³/36 + (1/2 bh)(2h/3)² = bh³/36 + 2bh³/9 = 9bh³/36 = bh³/4.

q: 11. The property of a material by which it can be drawn to smaller section, due to tension, is called
explain: Ductility is the property that allows a material to undergo significant plastic deformation under tensile stress, commonly observed when drawing metal into wires.

q: 12. As the elastic limit reaches, tensile strain
explain: Once the material surpasses the limit of proportionality and reaches the elastic limit/yield point, the strain increases significantly even with small increases in stress due to plastic flow.

q: 13. The stress necessary to initiate yielding, is considerably
options: more than that necessary to continue it
explain: In materials like mild steel, there is an Upper Yield Point (to initiate yielding) and a Lower Yield Point (to continue it). The stress to start yielding is higher than the stress required to maintain the yielding process.

q: 14. The deformation per unit length is called
explain: Strain is the dimensionless measure of deformation, calculated as the change in dimension divided by the original dimension.

q: 15. Strain is equal to
explain: By definition, strain (ε) is the ratio of change in length (δl) to the original length (l).

q: 16. When a body is subjected to two equal and opposite pulls and as a result the body tends to extend its length, the stress and strain induced is
explain: An external 'pull' results in a tensile internal resistance (stress) and a corresponding elongation (tensile strain).

q: 17. When a body is subjected to two equal and opposite forces, acting tangentially across the resisting section, as a result of which the body tends to shear off across the section, the stress and strain induced is
explain: Tangential forces acting across a section produce shear stress and a resulting angular deformation known as shear strain.

q: 18. Which of the following is a proper sequence?
options: proportional limit, elastic limit, yielding, failure
elastic limit, proportional limit, yielding, failure
explain: In a standard stress-strain curve for mild steel, the material first reaches the limit of proportionality, then the elastic limit, followed by yielding, and finally fracture/failure.

q: 19. Whenever a material is loaded within elastic limit, stress is ................ strain.
explain: This is the core definition of Hooke's Law: within the elastic range, stress varies linearly with strain.

q: 20. When a change in length takes place, the strain is known as
explain: Linear strain (or longitudinal strain) refers to the deformation occurring along the axis of the applied force.

q: 21. The change in length due to a tensile or compressive force acting on a body is given by
explain: From $\sigma = E \epsilon$, we get $P/A = E(\delta l/l)$. Rearranging for change in length gives $\delta l = Pl/AE$.

q: 22. The elongation of a conical bar under its own weight is ................ that of a prismatic bar of same length.
explain: The elongation of a conical bar due to self-weight is $\gamma l^2 / 6E$, which is exactly $1/3$ of the prismatic bar's elongation ($\gamma l^2 / 2E$).

q: 23. Every direct stress is always accompanied by a strain in its own direction and an opposite kind of strain in every direction at right angles to it. Such a strain is known as
explain: Lateral strain occurs perpendicular to the direction of the applied load. If a bar is stretched, it shortens in its transverse dimensions.

q: 24. The ratio of shear modulus to the modulus of elasticity for a Poisson's ratio of 0.4 will be
explain: Using the relation E = 2G(1 + μ). If μ = 0.4, then E = 2G(1.4) = 2.8G. Therefore, G/E = 1/2.8 = 5/14.

q: 25. In a bar of large length when held vertically, its own weight produces additional stress. The maximum stress will be
options: at every point of the bar
explain: The top cross-section must support the weight of the entire bar below it, making the stress maximum at the support.

q: 26. If the stress produced by a prismatic bar is equal to the working stress, the area of the cross-section becomes
explain: This refers to the theoretical 'limit of length' for a bar under its own weight; if the self-weight stress equals the allowed stress, any increase in length would require an infinite area to maintain that stress level.

q: 27. If all the dimensions of a bar are increased in the proportion n:1, the proportion of maximum stress will increase in the ratio
explain: Stress due to self-weight is σ = γL. If all dimensions increase by n, the new length is nL, so stress becomes n(γL), a ratio of n:1.

q: 28. The percentage elongation of a material from a direct tensile test indicates
explain: Ductility is the property that allows a material to undergo significant plastic deformation before rupture, measured by percentage elongation.

q: 29. The product of Young's modulus (E) and moment of inertia (I) is known as
explain: Flexural rigidity (EI) represents the resistance offered by a beam section against bending deformation.

q: 30. The region of the cross-section of a column in which compressive load may be applied without producing any tensile stress, is known as the core... in circular columns the radius of the core, is
explain: To avoid tension in a circular section (Middle Fourth Rule), the eccentricity must not exceed D/8 from the center, making the radius of the core R/4 (or D/8).

q: 31. A principal plane is a plane which carries
options: the given of higher magnitude acting
explain: By definition, principal planes are those on which the shear stress is zero; they only carry normal stresses (principal stresses).

q: 32. A prismatic bar is supported at top and is subjected to its own weight... the total elongation of the bar is given by
explain: The elongation due to self-weight is WL/2AE. Substituting W = ρAL, we get (ρAL)L/2AE = ρl²/2E.

q: 33. The ratio of maximum shear stress to average shear stress in the case of a rectangular section is
explain: As noted in Q. 301, the maximum shear stress for a rectangle is 1.5 times (3/2) the average shear stress.

q: 34. An element is subjected to two normal stress σ1 and σ2... The max shear stress is given by
explain: The maximum in-plane shear stress is equal to half the difference between the principal stresses: τ_max = (σ1 - σ2)/2.

q: 35. A body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane. The shear stress is maximum at a section inclined at ............ to the normal of the section.
explain: Shear stress is (σ/2) sin 2θ. This is maximum when sin 2θ = 1 (at 2θ = 90° or 270°), giving θ = 45° and 135°.

q: 36. Strain energy is the
options: energy stored in a body when strained within elastic limits
energy stored in a body when strained upto the breaking of a specimen
maximum strain energy which can be stored in a body
proof resilience per unit volume of a material
explain: As defined in Q. 327, it is the energy absorbed by a material when it is deformed elastically.

q: 37. When a member is subjected to twisting moment the stress in any elemental ring will be proportional to ............
options: Modulus of rigidity of the material
explain: According to the torsion formula $\frac{\tau}{r} = \frac{T}{J}$, shear stress ($\tau$) is directly proportional to the radial distance ($r$) from the center.

q: 38. The diamond quadrilateral pyramid indenter is used in ............
explain: The Vickers hardness test uses a square-based diamond pyramid indenter with an angle of 136° between opposite faces.

q: 39. The compression test is commonly used for testing ............
explain: Brittle materials (like concrete, cast iron, or stone) are much stronger in compression than tension, making compression tests standard for them.

q: 40. What is strain energy?
options: the energy stored in a body because of being strained
the energy that is spent for straining a body
explain: Strain energy is the internal work done by external forces while deforming a body, which is stored as potential energy.

q: 41. Dead load of a member is the
options: one that occurs due to dead body
one that comes all of a sudden
one that comes due to self weight of the object
explain: Dead load is the permanent self-weight of the structure/member itself.

q: 42. If all the dimensions of a bar are increased in the proportion n:1, the maximum stress produced in the prismatic bar by its own weight will increase in the ratio
explain: Self-weight stress scales linearly with the linear dimension scale factor n, giving a ratio of n:1.

q: 43. If magnitude and direction of a load does not change with respect to time, this type of load is called
explain: A load constant in magnitude and direction over time is a static load.

q: 44. The compression test is commonly used for testing
explain: Brittle materials (like cast iron, concrete) are typically much stronger in compression, so compression tests are standard for them.

q: 45. The brittle materials have low toughness because they
options: undergo large plastic deformation before failure
undergo small plastic deformation before failure
undergo no plastic deformation before failure
explain: Low toughness in brittle materials results from very limited plastic deformation absorbing energy before fracture.

q: 46. Centre of gravity of a semi circle is ___ above the base AB (diameter)
explain: Standard result: centroid of a semicircular area lies at 4r/3π from the diameter.

q: 47. The algebraic sum of the shear flow of a section in any direction must be equal to
explain: Shear flow forms a self-balancing internal system, summing to zero around a closed section.

q: 48. The maximum number of transverse shear forces possible at one end of an element of a plane frame are
explain: At each joint of a plane frame element, up to two transverse shear components can exist (in-plane, general loading).

q: 49. As per elastic theory of design the factor of safety is the ratio of
options: ultimate load to load at yield
explain: Factor of safety (elastic design) = yield stress / working (permissible) stress.

q: 50. The value of Poisson's ratio always remains
explain: For all real engineering materials, Poisson's ratio lies between 0 and 0.5, always less than one.

q: 51. Normally the numerical value of Poisson's ratio is
explain: Typical values: steel ≈ 0.3, concrete ≈ 0.15.

q: 52. Which of the following is a relatively ductile material?
explain: Mild steel shows large plastic elongation before fracture, making it relatively ductile compared to the brittle options listed.

q: 53. A member which is subjected to reversible tensile or compressible stress may fail at a stress lower than the ultimate stress of the material. The property of metal, is called
explain: Failure under repeated/reversed stress below the ultimate stress is the fatigue phenomenon.

q: 54. If the value of Young's Modulus of elasticity for a material is zero, it implies that the material is
explain: Zero stiffness against elastic deformation implies the material deforms permanently/plastically under any stress.

q: 55. Limit of proportionality depends upon
explain: The proportional limit is a material property, varying with the type of material.

q: 56. Which of the following is dimensionless?
explain: Strain is a ratio of length change to original length — dimensionless.

q: 57. The Young's Modulus of elasticity is defined as a ratio of stress & strain within the
explain: Hooke's Law (and hence E) is valid only within the elastic limit.

q: 58. Which of the following gives Modulus of Rigidity?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explain: Modulus of Rigidity (N/G) = shear stress / shear strain.

q: 59. Which of the following gives Bulk Modulus?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
ratio of the normal stress of equal magnitude on all six faces on a solid cube to the volumetric strain
explain: Bulk Modulus (K) = uniform normal stress / volumetric strain.

q: 60. Identify the correct relationship that exists among the modulus of elasticity (E), modulus of rigidity (N) and bulk modulus (k)
explain: Standard elastic-constants relation: E = 9KN / (3K + N).

q: 61. Normal strain is defined as
options: strain that is normal to shear strain
explain: Normal (linear) strain = change in length / original length.

q: 62. Shear strain is defined as
options: change in angle between planes at right angles
change in angles between two angles
explain: Shear strain is the change in the right angle between two originally perpendicular planes/lines.

q: 63. What is strain energy?
options: energy that is spent for straining a body
energy stored in a body because of being strained
explain: Strain energy is the elastic energy stored within a body as a result of deformation.

q: 64. The strain energy stored by a member when strained within elastic limit, is known as
explain: Resilience is the strain energy stored (and recoverable) within the elastic range.

q: 65. When equal and opposite forces applied to a body tend to elongate it, the stress produced is called
explain: Forces that pull a body apart (elongating it) produce tensile stress.

q: 66. The ratio of change in volume to the original volume is called:
explain: Volumetric strain = change in volume / original volume, by definition.

q: 67. Fatigue is the failure of a material under:
options: constant loads but occasionally well above static load
varying loads well below ultimate static load
constant loads well below ultimate static load
varying loads well above ultimate static load
explain: Fatigue failure occurs from repeated/varying stress cycles, even when each individual cycle's stress is well below the material's ultimate static strength.

q: 68. If a rod is simultaneously pulled at both of its ends, it will be a case of:
explain: Equal and opposite pulling forces along the rod's axis constitute axial (tensile) loading.

q: 69. Tensile internal force tends to:
explain: Tensile force pulls the member apart, causing elongation.

q: 70. The forces which meet at one point but their lines of action do not lie in a plane, are called:
explain: Forces meeting at a single point (concurrent) but spread across different planes (non-coplanar) are non-coplanar concurrent forces.

q: 71. The total time of collision and restitution of two bodies, is called
explain: The combined duration of the compression and restitution phases of a collision is called the period of impact.

q: 72. Mathematically, strain may be defined as
explain: Linear strain = change in length / original length, i.e. deformation per unit length.
